turns.text: The previous story examined Neuromancer and AI Escape in Cyberspace. Now the camera turns to The Lisp Machine Market Collapse and a new question along the same timeline: If we take The Lisp Machine Market Collapse apart, which idea truly changed the direction of research?

The 1980s expert-system boom created demand for specialized Lisp hardware and knowledge-engineering tools. The collapse mattered because it translated technical disappointment into layoffs, failed vendors and a stigma around the AI label.
That sounds like a promising direction. What mechanism actually makes it work?

The emotional mechanism is commercial overhang: a story of inevitable AI productivity becomes fragile when cheaper platforms undercut its infrastructure. Once users can run useful tools elsewhere, specialized AI hardware loses its aura.

Experts generally treat the late-1980s market collapse as a major signal of the second AI winter. Its legacy is a warning that AI enthusiasm depends on economics, maintainability and platform timing as much as on algorithms.
Seen alongside Neuromancer and AI Escape in Cyberspace, The Lisp Machine Market Collapse reveals how the same technical question can echo across different eras.
